title: Beijing Puts Its Own AI Models on the Export-Control List
subhead: China's Commerce and Science ministries propose licensing AI weights, chip designs and cluster tech above compute thresholds, while Seoul's memory giants quietly upgrade their plants inside China and Japan moves to certify data centers over China risk.

sections.heading: China Proposes Export Controls on Its Own AI
sections.body:
China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology released Announcement 48 of 2026 on Oct. 16, proposing 40 additions to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 14 of them outright prohibitions (J codes) and 26 licensing requirements (X codes), according to a ChinaTalk analysis published Oct. 21. Beijing opened a month of public comment, and separately imposed an immediate interim pre-export registration requirement on all 40 items — a mechanism with no precedent in earlier revisions of the catalogue.

The AI provisions target model weights and private IP — checkpoints, training code, architecture design, inference optimization — for models above any of three thresholds: 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, 2 trillion parameters, or capability judged 'globally leading.' ChinaTalk notes the 10^26 figure is identical to the threshold in the 2023 US executive order and the 2025 AI Diffusion rule's ECCN 4E091. The draft also covers AI chip design, memory chip technology, agent frameworks, AI-content detectors, training data and cyber capabilities, plus an unexpected entry on minority-language data.

The registration triggers matter as much as the codes. They capture IP sales, outbound licensing, and changes of ownership or actual controller to a foreign entity. ChinaTalk reads this as codifying the Manus case, in which a MOFCOM-led review forced the reversal of Meta's purchase of the Singapore-relocated Chinese agent startup — redomiciling abroad would no longer let a company escape Chinese jurisdiction.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is treating model weights as a strategic export the way it treats rare earth processing. For Chinese labs that built global adoption on open weights, the licensing regime is a direct constraint on their main growth strategy.

sections.heading: Nvidia's Supply Chain Is Now a Balance-Sheet Problem
sections.body:
At GTC Berlin, Nvidia said 'capacity is the constraint' — CEO Jensen Huang's words — and put money behind it. The company plans to expand substrate capacity for its products 2.5x over three years, adding Samsung Electro-Mechanics as a substrate supplier with immediate capacity in South Korea; by 2028 roughly a quarter of Samsung's substrate output is to go to Nvidia, The Register reported. Existing suppliers IBIDEN (Japan) and Unimicron (Taiwan) get plant expansions and capacity reservations, and Korean packaging firm Amkor signed a capacity reservation.

Nvidia also unveiled DSX pods — 28-metric-ton containers holding seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks (504 GPUs, 252 Vera CPUs), built with HPE, Dell and Schneider Electric. Nvidia claims they cut data center deployment from six months to about two weeks, with first units rolling out early next year.

Alongside the hardware, Nvidia shipped open-weight models aimed squarely at European sovereign-AI buyers: refreshed Nemotron Retriever embedding and reranking models (1B to 8B parameters, 34 languages, NVFP4 quantized for Blackwell) plus a Nemotron Parse model for PDFs and charts.
sections.whyItMatters: The bottleneck in AI hardware has moved from chip design to substrates, packaging and deployment speed. Nvidia is now effectively underwriting its suppliers' capex, and selling open weights as the answer to Europe's demand for AI it doesn't have to fully trust Washington to keep supplying.

sections.heading: Samsung and SK Hynix Upgrade Their Plants Inside China
sections.body:
Reuters reported exclusively that Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading their Chinese plants to produce more advanced memory chips, citing people familiar with the matter — investments that proceed under existing US export curbs rather than in defiance of them. Syndicated coverage (Benzinga, Yahoo Finance, TweakTown) framed the upgrades as a response to AI-driven memory demand and to pressure from Chinese competitor YMTC closing the gap in NAND.

The picture is of a policy equilibrium that both Washington and Seoul can live with: the memory majors keep older-node capacity inside China serving Chinese customers, while the most advanced lines stay in Korea. Note that the original Reuters report was not directly accessible for this brief; details here rest on the syndicated summaries.
sections.whyItMatters: Export controls have not stopped Korean memory investment in China — they have shaped what node it runs at. As Chinese domestic suppliers improve, that line becomes harder to hold.

sections.heading: Frontier AI Can Now Plan Attacks on Power and Water Systems
sections.body:
Research firm Frenos published findings that frontier AI models successfully planned cyberattacks against operational technology (OT) — water and power systems — in roughly 90% of attempts, with some reporting citing up to 93% of tests. Business Wire's release on the research carries the headline finding that critical infrastructure may have about two years before AI can reliably plan attacks on OT. Anadolu Agency, Axios and Industrial Cyber all covered the results; Booz Allen separately warned that frontier models can exploit OT pathways, manipulate controllers and move robotic equipment.

These are simulation results against test environments, not evidence of attacks in the field. But they land against a live backdrop of attacks on utilities — including Iranian intrusions into water systems and a French refrigeration incident cited by trade coverage.
sections.whyItMatters: The binding constraint on OT attacks used to be scarce human expertise. If general-purpose models can close that gap in about two years, the security calculus for every exposed municipal utility changes — and so does the case for treating AI capability as a defense question.

sections.heading: Japan Builds a Certification Wall Around Its Compute
sections.body:
Nikkei reported that Tokyo will establish a certification system for data centers and cloud services, assessing risk management and equipment procurement sources, and will urge finance, healthcare and other key sectors toward certified infrastructure. The stated aim is to encourage secure technology while blocking risk from China, Russia and 'other countries of concern.'

Separately, Nikkei reported that Japan's growth strategy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will prioritize semiconductors and video games as near-term wins, with AI-controlled robots and hydrogen as longer-term bets; the first five-year roadmap is due by year-end.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is turning 'sovereign AI' from a procurement slogan into a certification gate. For non-Japanese cloud and data center operators, procurement provenance — not just data location — becomes a market-access question.

sections.heading: China Widens Export Controls to Dredgers and Tunnel Borers
sections.body: China's Commerce Ministry said it will impose export controls on tunnel boring machines starting Nov. 18, requiring licenses under dual-use export-control rules, Reuters reported via Nikkei. The ministry also adjusted controls on drone-related items and dredgers. India is the implicit target: it relies heavily on imported TBMs for metro and highway construction, and China is among the main suppliers. ChinaTalk notes port dredgers and tunnel borers sit in the same announcement wave as the AI and photovoltaic additions.
sections.whyItMatters: This is control applied to civil construction equipment, not cutting-edge tech. It shows Beijing willing to use mundane industrial dominance as leverage — and it lands on India's infrastructure pipeline specifically.

sections.heading: Space: China's Low-Inclination Constellation Takes Shape
sections.body:
A commercial Ceres-1 solid rocket launched from the Dongfang Hangtiangang sea launch platform off Rizhao, Shandong, on Oct. 21, carrying the first satellite of the Wuyang remote sensing constellation, SpaceNews reported. Wuyang is a Guangzhou-backed project targeting low-inclination orbits — described in Chinese coverage as filling an observation gap over the Earth's 'golden belt,' the heavily populated tropical and subtropical band that sun-synchronous constellations cover less densely.

In Taiwan, TASA launched two more satellites in its CubeSat program (Taipei Times).
sections.whyItMatters: Most commercial Earth-observation capacity is optimized for mid-latitude, sun-synchronous coverage. A dedicated low-inclination constellation over the tropics is a commercial play with obvious intelligence value for a region where Chinese infrastructure and maritime interests are concentrated.

bottomLine: Beijing spent the week converting its own industrial strengths into formal export levers — drafting licenses over frontier AI weights and restricting tunnel boring machines for India — while Nvidia responded to the same strategic competition by financially propping up its substrate and packaging suppliers and courting European sovereign-AI buyers with open-weight models. The clearest signal is that control is moving from controlling what you can buy to controlling what you can sell: China is now restricting its own model exports, and Japan is certifying data centers by where their equipment comes from.
sources: ChinaTalk, The Register, Reuters (via Nikkei Asia and syndication), Nikkei Asia, SpaceNews, Business Wire/Frenos, Anadolu Agency, Axios, Industrial Cyber, Taipei Times, Benzinga, Yahoo Finance, TweakTown
